fields.sections.1.exchanges.1.con.words: Joshua Bowen argues that Exodus and Leviticus distinguish Israelite debt service from foreign lifelong property, allowing corporal punishment, purchase, and inherited ownership.
fields.sections.1.exchanges.1.con.critique: Strongest feature: Bowen grounds the negative case in Exodus’s beating and injury rules, owner compensation after an ox goring, and Leviticus’s express permission to buy foreigners, hold them permanently, and transmit them as inherited property. Principal limitation: His antebellum-South analogy exceeds the evidence presented, while the differing provisions for Israelite debt servants, sold daughters, and foreign slaves complicate any characterization of a single biblical regime. Live burden: He must establish why these legally authorized inequalities make biblical treatment morally indefensible despite release, provisioning, and injury protections, not simply show that the texts regulated several coercive statuses. Locked score: The fixed 89 recognizes precise, convergent textual warrant for ownership and coercion, while deducting for an underdeveloped historical analogy and an incompletely explicit bridge from legal description to moral verdict.
